title: [AMD][GFX1250] TDM copy reordering in the pipeliner
body:
* [AMD][GFX1250] TDM copy reordering in the pipeliner

Summary

Adds a scheduling variant to the AMD stream pipeliner that reorders TDM-fed loop bodies for better async overlap. The new schedule issues all async_tdm_copy_global_to_local operations first, followed by an async_tdm_wait, then the local loads and dot -- improving latency hiding.

Motivation

The previous schedule issued async_tdm_wait first, then interleaved async_tdm_copy_global_to_local and local_load operations, followed by the dot. This had two key drawbacks:
- Global loads were issued after the waitcnt, draining the current copies before the next were issued and effectively serializing consecutive iterations' copies.
- There're explicit barriers between async_tdm_copy_global_to_local and local_load operations.

The new schedule addresses both issues: by issuing global loads before the waitcnt, the waitcnt latency can be hidden. This is especially beneficial in the memory-bound regime, where the current TDM copies may overlap with the next TDM copies on the TDM engine. Additionally, the barriers between async_tdm_copy_global_to_local and local_load are removed naturally. Note that removing the barriers alone only yields a 3-5% improvement; the majority of the gain comes from issuing global loads before waitcnt.

Performance

- The reordering yields a 10-29% improvement in Triton MXFP GEMM performance on GFX1250;
- After reordering, triton performance reaches 80-100% of Gluon performance on GFX1250.

Details

- The reordering is currently gated behind the TRITON_HIP_DISABLE_TDM_REORDER flag (off by default).
- Adds a lit test.

title: [WIP] [AMD][BACKEND] Emit packed scaled_upcast layout for dot decomposition
body:
**This is still work in progress**

## Description

`amdgpu.scaled_upcast` requires a layout which has `groupSize` (min 4) elements along `axis` held by a thread. When doing software emulation for scaled_dot we currently emit a blocked layout invalidating this requirement and rely on RemoveLayoutConversation to fix this for us. 
With https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11760 this no longer reliably works and this PR emits an legal packed initial layout. We also treat it as a layout anchor to avoid invalidating the layouts with RemoveLayoutConversions.

This also allows us to have a proper verifier to ensure the layouts are compatible and we no longer trigger late asserts when lowering to llvm. The other option would be to implement a software path were we lower via unpacked instructions, but it would silently regress performance if we mess up the layouts, especially in Gluon.

## Known issues
This will break if the axis dimension is too small so we do not have enough unique elements along `axis`. This is a latent bug and would trigger an assert in the lowering before this PR (it's now a verifier fail). This will be fixed in a follow up PR.

title: [AMD] Fix RDNA DRAM bandwidth estimates
body:
## Summary

`get_dram_gbps()` computes peak bandwidth as memory clock × bus width × 2,
which assumes two data transfers per clock.

The HIP driver reports the DRAM clock and bus width correctly, but current RDNA
products use GDDR6 or LPDDR5X. Their effective memory data rates require larger
transfer multipliers:

- gfx1100, gfx1101, gfx1102, gfx1200 and gfx1201 use GDDR6: 16 transfers per clock
- gfx1151 uses LPDDR5X: 8 transfers per clock

Use the normalized Triton target architecture to select the RDNA multiplier.
CUDA, CDNA and unknown HIP architectures retain the existing ×2 behavior.

gfx1150 and gfx1152 are intentionally excluded because their platforms may use
either DDR5 or LPDDR5X, which cannot be distinguished from the properties
currently exposed to this helper.

## Validation

Runtime properties and resulting peak bandwidth:

| Architecture| Current formula | With this change | Published value |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| gfx1100 | 107.904 GB/s | 863.232 GB/s | 864 GB/s |
| gfx1151 | 64 GB/s | 256 GB/s | 256 GB/s |
| gfx1200 | 40.256 GB/s | 322.048 GB/s | up to 320 GB/s |

Runtime validation covers gfx1100, gfx1151 and gfx1200. The gfx1101, gfx1102
and gfx1201 cases are based on current AMD product documentation and synthetic
driver properties rather than local hardware.

gfx1200 reports a 1258 MHz memory clock at runtime rather than the nominal
1250 MHz used by the public specification, accounting for the 0.64% difference.

A new table-driven unit test covers every mapped architecture, both documented
gfx1151 bus widths, and unchanged CUDA behavior. Seven HIP cases fail with the
old ×2 formula while the CUDA control passes; all eight pass with this change.
The test uses synthetic driver properties and runs without GPU hardware.

title: [TensorDescriptor] Allow backends to specialize descriptor arguments
body:
`specialize_tensordesc` returns no specialization key for any backend, so a descriptor is the only kernel argument a backend cannot key on, despite carrying a base pointer plus per-dimension shapes and strides.

Mirror what tensors already have (`supports_native_tensor_specialization` and `get_tensor_specialization`) with `supports_native_tensordesc_specialization` and `get_tensordesc_specialization`, same opt-out semantics.

Both in-tree backends inherit the flag as set, so the key stays `None` and the hook is never called. 
It is meant for backends that do need to key on descriptor properties, including ones shipped out of tree as an extension.

title: Emit scheduling DAG as a (bb, position) edge list from translate_to_mir
body:
Replaces the old `dump_sched_dag` path with a scheduling DAG emitted directly from the MIR that `translate_to_mir` already dumps. The old path ran a second, independently-scheduled compilation and printed `-misched-print-dags` text that keyed instructions by register name, which is fragile across virtual-register
  renumbering. The new path appends a per-region edge list after the `SCHEDULING DAG` marker in the MIR dump:

```
  region <bb>
  node <pos> <def-reg|-> <opcode>
  edge <src-pos> <dst-pos> <Type> <latency> [<reg>]
```

Instruction identity is `(bb, position)`, so the MIR dump and the DAG stay correlatable regardless of how vregs are numbered. Data/Anti/Output/Memory/Barrier edges are kept; Artificial/Cluster are dropped.

`DAGBuilder` is a thin wrapper over LLVM's `ScheduleDAGInstrs`. It runs as a `MachineFunctionPass` so `LiveIntervals` is available; that lets `buildSchedGraph` track lane masks and produce **subregister-precise** dependencies that match LLVM's own scheduler (without LI, subregister defs/uses are over-approximated and the DAG gains spurious WAW/WAR edges).

The DAG is currently built by re-parsing the dumped MIR text. A subsequent commit will build it from the live pipeline `MachineFunction` instead, avoiding the re-parse round-trip and reusing the pipeline's `LiveIntervals`.

title: [AMD][GLUON] Expose sched barrier
body: Expose `ttgl.amd.hint.sched_barrier` in Gluon to control LLVM scheduling behavior for AMD. `sched_barrier` prevents LLVM's instruction scheduler from moving instructions across this point.

title: [FRONTEND] Promote same-type fp8 arithmetic to fp16
body:
## Summary

Same-type fp8 arithmetic (`x + y`, `x - y`, `x * y`, unary `-x`, comparisons, `tl.sum`) passed the frontend and died at the LLVM verifier, because rule 6 in `computation_type_impl` kept same-type fp8 as fp8 and no backend can lower those ops at fp8.

Following option (b) from the issue discussion (endorsed by the reporter): promote before evaluating, like the div/mod rule already does. Same-type fp8 arithmetic now computes in fp16:

- `computation_type_impl` gains an `fp8_arith` flag; the same-type fp8 branch returns fp16 when it is set.
- `add`, `sub`, `mul`, the six comparisons, and unary `minus` set it; `tl.sum` picks fp16 for fp8 inputs in `_pick_sum_dtype`.
- Selection ops that lower at fp8 (`tl.maximum`, `tl.minimum`, `tl.where`, `clamp`) keep fp8. Mixed fp8 operands keep their existing fp16 rule. Div/mod keep their fp32 rule.

Fixes #11898

## Tests

`test_fp8_div_mod_promotion` moves its two pins to fp16 (`x * y`, `x * 2.0`). New `test_fp8_arith_promotes_to_fp16` pins the dtype of each promoted op plus the TTIR evidence (fp16 `arith.cmpf` operands, `tt.fp_to_fp` before the fp16 reduce body, fp16 `negf`), and pins maximum/minimum/where staying fp8.

Local run (macOS arm64, no GPU): `test_frontend.py` 681/681 pass including the new test; `test_compile_only`/`test_annotations`/`test_tuple`/`test_module` pass except the CUDA-launch cases, which fail identically on the base tree here (no CUDA on this host). GPU-side numeric behavior is not covered locally; the change is frontend type promotion, and the pins above verify what reaches the backend.

title: [DO NOT MERGE] Investigate PTX lowering of 1.0 as 1
body:
## Summary

The NVIDIA cache-policy lowering prints a full `f32` fraction (`1.0`) as `1` inside inline Parallel Thread Execution (PTX) assembly. The assembler rejects that integer-looking operand for `createpolicy.fractional`.

Add a `newConstantOperand(double)` overload to the PTX builder using `std::to_chars` for the shortest round-tripping decimal representation. Append `.0` when the representation has neither a decimal point nor an exponent, and use the formatter for cache-policy fractions. This applies to integral-valued floats generally, including `2.0`; it does not special-case `1.0`. Round trips preserve binary64 precision, as in Python. The f32 cache-policy fraction widens exactly to double before formatting: `0.1f` therefore prints as `0.10000000149011612`, while `0.1` prints as `0.1`. An integral forwarding overload preserves existing integer calls without ambiguity.

This is an investigation draft and must not be merged yet. The source audit found one direct `APFloat::toString` call in NVIDIA PTX lowering; this is not a claim that all inline-assembly constants have been audited.

## Desired features

- Finite double constants retain their value when parsed back as double; float inputs widen exactly.
- Integral-valued constants remain unmistakably floating point, including signed zero.
- Cache-policy fraction `1.0` compiles successfully, preserving the existing behavior of fractional and legacy policies.

## Validation

Hardware: NVIDIA GB300 on Linux.

- `make`
- `TestPtxAsmFormat` in the build directory's `third_party/nvidia/unittest/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/`
- `lit -v test/Conversion/tritongpu_to_llvm.mlir` from the build directory
- `python -m pytest -s --tb=short python/test/gluon/test_core.py::test_async_copy_mbarrier`
- A standalone copy-kernel comparison using fractions `0.5`, `1.0`, and the legacy eviction policy, with exact output comparison and generated PTX inspection.

title: [FRONTEND][NV] Skip zero-result ops when picking the reduce combiner
body:
Fixes #11937.

## What breaks

`ReduceOpConversion` took the first op of the combine region as the combiner and asked the target for its reduction-tree arity; the NVIDIA `getReductionTreeArity` dereferences `combinerOp->getResult(0)` unconditionally. A `tt.print` (or any zero-result op) in front of the arithmetic combiner aborts assertions builds and reads past the result list in release builds.

## Fix

Walk the region and use the first op that has results as the combiner for the arity query; when no resultful op exists, fall back to arity 2 (a binary tree), which is valid for any target. Standard reduces are unchanged: their first op is the arithmetic combiner, so the selection is byte-identical there.

## Testing

- New lit case in `test/Conversion/reduce_to_llvm.mlir` (`@reduce_with_print_in_combine`): a `tt.print` ahead of `arith.addi` in the combine region; the module must convert instead of crashing.
- NOT RUN locally: this machine has no `triton-opt` build (a full LLVM toolchain build is beyond what I can justify for this diff), so the lit case is verified by structure and reviewed against the existing print/reduce cases in-tree, but it has not been executed here. CI runs the suite; the failure mode it guards is a compile-time crash in the pass, so the lit run is the meaningful gate.
- AMD's `getReductionTreeArity` never touches results (per the issue), so the selection change is behavior-neutral there.

title: [TUTORIALS] Avoid per-case streams in fused-softmax benchmark
body:
Fixes #11661

The fused-softmax tutorial created and selected a new PyTorch device stream in every `benchmark()` call. This made each case use a different stream while the caching allocator retained memory from earlier cases, causing reserved memory to grow through the sweep.

Remove the two per-case stream calls so the benchmark uses the current stream. On an 8 GiB RTX 2000 Ada running Windows, the full 294-case sweep completed with this change alone. Reserved memory still grew (to 23,016 MiB under WDDM), so this does not establish that the original 6 GiB OOM is fixed on that card.

title: [BACKEND] Lower float % to libdevice fmod on NVIDIA
body:
On NVIDIA, `%` on floating-point tensors is lowered to `llvm.frem`, and NVPTX expands that to `x - trunc(x / y) * y`. Once `x / y` cannot be represented exactly the result is wrong, even though `%` follows C `fmod` semantics: e.g. `1e10 % 3` returns 256 instead of 1 in fp32, `3e7 % 0.7` returns -0.289 instead of 0.411, and fp64 is affected the same way. `torch.fmod` on the same device gives the correct results.

This lowers `arith.remf` on NVIDIA to libdevice's `__nv_fmodf`/`__nv_fmod` (fp16/bf16 go through fp32), and adds `test_fmod_large_quotient`, which fails on main for fp32 and fp64.

title: [AMD] Do not stagger CDNA4 padded layouts over rows that do not exist
body:
`composePaddedLayoutForAsyncCopyCDNA4` aborts the compiler for any dot operand whose contiguous row spans more than a warp of vectors. Downstream in [ROCm/rocmlirTriton](https://github.com/ROCm/rocmlirTriton) this took down a whole CI tuning stage on gfx950: a generated GEMM kernel with a 1x2048 f16 A tile died on `PaddedSharedEncodingAttr::verify` with "Broadcasting in offset dimension is not supported".

The function divides `warpSize` by `contigLanes` in two places. Once `contigLanes > warpSize` that quotient truncates to zero and both guards that depend on it stop working. `requiredRows` collapses to zero, so `xWayConflicts` always reports one and the "too few rows to stagger" path never triggers. The `useBestWrap` condition degenerates to `nonContigDim >= 0`, which is always true.

`wrap` is then forced to 16 even for a tile with a single row. Bases are added for rows 1, 2, 4 and 8 that the tile does not have, the resulting linear layout broadcasts in the offset dimension, and the verifier rejects it. In an assertions build that aborts rather than falling back to a layout that would have worked.

This compares both guards scaled by `contigLanes` instead of dividing `warpSize` by it, and additionally requires at least `bestWrap` rows before staggering over that many.

The added lit test is the failing case reduced to a dot whose A operand is a single row of 2048 f16 elements, which is 256 vectors of 8 against a warp size of 64. It aborts `triton-opt` without this change and passes with it. The failing call chain is `PipelinePass` -> `expandLoops` -> `lowerLoops` -> `lowerLoop` -> `getSharedEncIfAllUsersAreDotEnc` -> `composePaddedLayout` -> `composePaddedLayoutForAsyncCopyCDNA4`.

One caveat worth stating: this fixes one of at least two causes behind that same broadcasting error. Across 70 shape and dtype combinations it takes aborts from 8 down to 3, and the 3 that remain reach the symptom through a different arithmetic path.

Reviewed internally at AMD as part of the downstream fix in https://github.com/ROCm/rocmlirTriton/pull/508.

title: [AMD] Fix partitioned shared and WMMA layouts for CGAs
body:
## Problem

Partitioned shared layouts were composed globally before applying the CGA mapping. This could interleave partition/group bits across CTAs instead of keeping each CTA’s physical partitions local.

Clustered WMMA lowering also derived repetition counts from the full CGA tile, causing block dimensions to produce redundant WMMA instructions. Broadcast CGA layouts could additionally make partitioned subslice lowering fail because their layouts are surjective but not square.

## Solution

- Compose partitioned shared layouts within each CTA, then add the CGA mapping.
- Validate that each per-CTA partition extent is divisible by all logical pieces.
- Use a pseudoinverse when recovering partition selection from broadcast layouts.
- Compute WMMA repetitions from the per-CTA layout and shape.
- Add regression tests for padded/swizzled layouts, physical-base rotation, and scaled/unscaled WMMA lowering.

## Testing

- Full Triton rebuild
- Partitioned-layout C++ unit tests
- 16 partition-related lit tests

All tests pass.

> This change was implemented, reviewed, and validated by GPT.

title: [AMD] Bypass the epilogue relayout for FMA
body:
`BypassEpilogueSMEM` only rewrites a store when the `convert_layout` feeding it is MMA (MFMA/WMMA), so FMA is silently skipped. That means that the expensive relayout stays, with its LDS round trip, which hurts performance. This PR replaces that bail-out with a profitability check, so the relayout can also be bypassed on FMA kernels when it is profitable. With this PR, we measured ~10% speedup on several FMA kernels.

Two layouts are involved in the decision:
1. The *candidate* layout is the `convert_layout` source (the one the store would pivot to if the relayout is dropped, **srcType in the code**)
2. The *current* layout is the coalesced one the store uses today (**dstType** in the code)

The heuristic for when the relayout is profitable for FMA is simple:
- Both layouts have the same contiguity? Bail out if not (we cannot compare those 2 layouts)
- Consecutive lanes of the candidate layout goes along that dimension? If not, the store would not be coalesced, so bail out
- Would skipping the relayout increase the store instruction? If yes, it will be bad for performance, so bail out

If all of those guards pass, then we conclude it's profitable to skip the relayout.

This PR also adds several testcases to exercise those situations.

title: [NVIDIA] Fix unhandled OSError crash in NvidiaTool.from_path triggered on macOS
body:
## Summary

Fix `NvidiaTool.from_path` to handle `OSError` (e.g., `Exec format error`) 
when the bundled NVIDIA binaries are not executable on the current platform.

This fixes a `make test-nogpu` regression on macOS introduced by #11806.

## Problem

On macOS, Triton's build system downloads Linux ARM64 (sbsa) NVIDIA binaries 
(ptxas, cuobjdump, etc.) because NVIDIA does not provide macOS-native CUDA 
toolchain. These Linux ELF binaries exist on disk but cannot be executed on 
macOS, raising `OSError: [Errno 8] Exec format error`.

`NvidiaTool.from_path` only caught `FileNotFoundError` (file missing) and 
`CalledProcessError` (non-zero exit), but not the more general `OSError` that 
covers format errors. Since `FileNotFoundError` is a subclass of `OSError`, 
replacing it with `OSError` is backward-compatible and also covers other 
potential OS-level errors like `PermissionError` on any platform.

This caused `test_gluon_ast_source_without_driver[target0-cubin]` to crash 
instead of being gracefully skipped.

## Changes

1. **`python/triton/knobs.py`**: Change `except (CalledProcessError, FileNotFoundError)` 
   to `except (CalledProcessError, OSError)` in `NvidiaTool.from_path`, so it 
   correctly returns `None` when the binary exists but is not executable.

2. **`python/test/gluon/test_frontend.py`**: Skip the CUDA parameterization of 
   `test_gluon_ast_source_without_driver` when `ptxas` is not available, using 
   the now-correct `RuntimeError` from `get_ptxas()`.

## Testing

Verified on macOS (Apple Silicon)

title: [BACKEND] Support fp8 <=> fp64 casts by going through fp32
body:
## Background
`x.to(tl.float8e4nv)` on an fp64 tensor (and `fp8.to(tl.float64)`) cannot compile on any target: the frontend emits `tt.fp_to_fp` between fp8 and f64, but neither backend lowers it.
- NVIDIA: `getConversionFunc` has no f64 entries and calls `report_fatal_error("Unsupported rounding mode for conversion.")`, which aborts the Python process.
- AMD: `failed to legalize operation 'tt.fp_to_fp'`.

Inductor emits exactly this for `x_fp64.to(torch.float8_e4m3fn)`.

```python
@triton.jit
def kernel(X, Z):
    offs = tl.arange(0, 128)
    tl.store(Z + offs, tl.load(X + offs).to(tl.float8e4nv))   # X: *fp64
```

## Summary
- NVIDIA and AMD `FpToFp` lowerings: an f64 source is truncated to f32 before the f32 -> fp8 conversion, and an fp8 -> f64 cast converts to f32 and extends. Only RTNE is supported for f64 -> fp8, as before for other rounding modes.
- Interpreter: `_convert_float`'s downcast rounded ties away from zero, dropped the carry when rounding overflowed the mantissa (126.24 -> fp8e4nv gave 64 instead of 128) and rounded subnormal results twice. It now rounds the mantissa once to nearest even, carries into the exponent, and keeps NaN as NaN. Two shifts also needed unsigned shift amounts for 64-bit types, so fp8 <=> fp64 works in the interpreter too.

## Tests
- Lit: `tritongpu_to_llvm_hopper.mlir` and `amd/fp_to_fp.mlir` check the f32 step in both directions (fail before, pass after).
- `test_core.py::test_cast`: fp8 <=> float64 added to the fp8 cast matrix.
- `test_core.py::test_cast_fp64_to_fp8_rounding`: a few doubles covering ties, rounding into the next binade and subnormals, compared bitwise with `torch.Tensor.to`; also runs in the interpreter.
- Interpreter downcasts checked exhaustively over all fp16/bf16 inputs and ~1.3M fp32 values against an exact reference for every fp8/fp16/bf16 target (RTNE and RTZ).
- H200 (sm90): the raw kernel and `torch.compile` (fp64 -> fp8e4nv, fp8 -> fp64) compile and match eager bit-for-bit; `test_core.py -k "test_cast or test_convert_float16_to_float32"` 170 passed, `test_conversions.py` 57 passed. A800 (sm80): fp64 <=> fp8e5 cases pass. The CI interpreter suite passes on Linux.

title: Gluon warp if upstream
body:
FA kernels can spend time rescaling register accumulators when their runtime scale is exactly one. A block-wide branch cannot skip work independently for warps owning different rows, and elementwise selection does not express the execution boundary needed to avoid that arithmetic. This adds `gl.warp_if` to request warp-level skipping while preserving the result of unconditional block-level evaluation.

```python
@gluon.jit
def rescale(acc, total, alpha):
    return acc * alpha[:, None], total * alpha

acc, total = gl.warp_if(alpha != 1, (acc, total), rescale, args=(alpha,))
```

A warp executes the complete body when any of its conditions is true; otherwise it retains its inputs. The compiler verifies that false-condition elements are identities. Thus layout changes can change the amount of skipped work, but cannot change the logical result. Conditions can describe rows, columns, or individual elements. No warp-varying source scalar or elementwise select is introduced.

The initial verifier accepts f32/f64 rescaling by the scale tested with `scale != 1`, identity returns, register-only broadcasts/expansions, and their supported canonicalized forms. It rejects effects, memory access, collectives, nested control flow, uninlined calls, incompatible layouts, and identities it cannot prove. All-true constant masks have no identity obligation but retain the body/layout restrictions. AMD flush-to-zero mode is rejected.

AMD and NVIDIA share a ballot/branch/phi lowering. The region remains visible through layout inference and GPU scheduling. LLVM may if-convert small bodies; final instruction selection is not an API guarantee. GSan and ConSan compilation are covered. FPSan validates the original body and evaluates it unconditionally before replacing arithmetic with hashes. Proton scopes can surround the operation; scopes inside its body are rejected.

## Performance evidence

The measurements below predate the latest rebase onto upstream `2cfa16702`.
Post-rebase regression checks and an FA correctness smoke test pass; performance
has not been remeasured on the new base.

On one gfx950 GPU, tutorial FA v4, BF16, B=32, H=8, N=8192, D=128, BM=256, BN=64, eight warps:

| Compiler | Unconditional MFMA efficiency | warp_if MFMA efficiency | Gain |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Stock LLVM | 62.10% | 69.91% | +7.81 pp |
| Tutorial scheduler | 71.59% | 84.62% | +13.03 pp |

These are medians of three interleaved ATT captures per variant. The tutorial metric is `4096 / measured main-loop cycles * 100`, accounting for two resident waves per SIMD, over 62 paired iterations. These measurements establish the use case, not a universal performance benefit.

The tuned measurements use the tutorial scheduler and its supporting hook, which are not included in this PR. The clean upstream branch also passes the full-size FA comparison against unconditional rescaling and an independent FP32 reference, with identical register/shared-memory use and no spills. A final clean-branch run measured 10.277 ms with `warp_if` versus 10.991 ms unconditionally, a 6.95% throughput gain (median of seven rounds of 40 prepared launches).

## Validation

- Rebased on 2026-09-23 onto upstream `2cfa16702a3ad04e3f4d4f34f4791c4ecfcde7e5` and rebuilt with Proton enabled (C++20).
- 86 focused tests passed: AMD/NVIDIA source compilation, identity/layout/effect rejection, constant masks, f32/f64 GPU execution, NaNs/subnormals/signed zeros, row/column/element masks, multiple results, loop reconvergence, and sanitizer integration.
- Complete Gluon frontend suite: 556 passed, 184 skipped.
- Complete MLIR suite: 302 passed, 2 expected failures.

- Proton instrumentation suite excluding the overhead benchmark: 26 passed, 8 skipped.
- `pre-commit run --from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD` passed.

The performance motivation and hardware validation in this proposal are scoped to AMD gfx950. NVIDIA compilation and MLIR lowering checks provide additional coverage; NVIDIA runtime validation and performance claims are outside this submission's scope.

title: [Gluon] Add linear asynchronous bulk loads to shared memory
body:
PR description written by Codex

Gluon currently needs inline PTX for linear global-to-shared bulk copies, hiding their memory dependencies from the compiler and sanitizers. Add `hopper.bulk.async_load(smem, pointer, num_bytes, barrier, pred=True, multicast=False)`, also exported from Blackwell and Rubin, with native IR and `cp.async.bulk` lowering.

The byte count is a positive compile-time multiple of 16 within a contiguous destination view; addresses must be 16-byte aligned, with a separate completion barrier in each CTA. Requires SM90+/PTX8.6+. ConSan tracks transaction counts and shared-memory completion, GSan tracks exact predicated source ranges, and IISan checks source alignment.

Other changes add documentation and regression coverage for layouts, partial copies, predication, 2/4-CTA partitioning and replication, multicast destinations, arrival routing, phase reuse, warp-specialized handoff, and sanitizer diagnostics. After rebuilding, all 24 affected compiler tests and 147 focused frontend/GPU/sanitizer cases passed on GB300, including code generation for SM90/100/103. The three GSan ordering cases also passed with line information disabled.

ConSan conservatively covers the entire destination view. GSan records source reads at issue time; its pre-existing gap in tracking asynchronous global-memory lifetime through completion remains unchanged.

title: [GSan] Add write_once allocations
body:
This adds a special "write-once" gsan allocation. The rules here are that they can be written exactly once, and read many times after being written. 

This means we only need to track for read-after-write violations, so we can simplify the shadow cell to a single scalar write clock which is 1/6th of the size of a normal shadow cell. This allows us to track byte-granularity while actually using less shadow memory than 4-byte granularity normal allocations.

Also, this allows for a completely wait-free shadow memory access pattern. This means we don't serialize accesses to those address.

title: Fix FP8 round-to-nearest conversions on NVIDIA
body:
Fix two NVIDIA paths that round FP8 conversions incorrectly: software E5M2 conversion before Ada, and FP32 conversion on Ada.

```python
# x.to(tl.float8e5, fp_downcast_rounding="rtne")
# FP16/BF16 input on the software path:
# x = 1.125:       main -> 1.25; this PR -> 1.0 (ties to even)

# x.to(tl.float8e4nv, fp_downcast_rounding="rtne")
# FP32 input on Ada:
# x = 1.0625001:   main -> 1.0;  this PR -> 1.125
```

The software path shares one nearest-even FP16 encoder. FP32 first uses round-to-odd, which keeps a bit recording discarded precision so the final round can distinguish an exact tie from either neighbor. BF16 can use the same encoder without changing the E5M2 rounding decision. Finite overflow saturates. Rounding and clamping before extracting the FP8 byte lets the compiler emit fewer shifts.

Ada converts directly from FP32: the old FP16 intermediate lost the bits that distinguish the second example from an exact tie. Tests cover ties and neighbors, subnormals, signed zero, overflow and NaNs.

The fix also enables existing E5M2 conversion, MXFP, reduction-gradient and matmul tests on A100. Remove their obsolete skips while keeping the actual E4M3 hardware requirements.

Independent fix, based on [main](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/tree/main).

title: [NVIDIA] Lower tensor-map proxy fences with NVVM
body:
## Summary

Replace the remaining supported compiler-generated inline NVIDIA fence with NVVM dialect operations.

The tensor-map acquire fence currently emits `fence.proxy.tensormap::generic.acquire.gpu` through inline PTX. Keeping this operation in NVVM exposes its synchronization semantics to MLIR and delegates PTX spelling and target validation to LLVM's NVPTX backend.

## Details

- Replace inline `fence.proxy.tensormap::generic.acquire.gpu` with `nvvm.fence.proxy.acquire`.
- Preserve first-warp predication with explicit LLVM control flow because the NVVM fence intrinsic is not predicated.
- Represent the fence's generic address explicitly with an address-space cast from the global tensor-map pointer.
- Preserve the existing inline `cp.async.bulk` PTXAS workaround unchanged.
- Preserve the final CTA synchronization barrier.

Other compiler-generated fence paths already use structured lowering:

- async/shared proxy fences use `nvvm.fence.proxy`;
- the mbarrier initialization fence is handled by #10937;
- atomic thread fences are represented by LLVM atomic ordering;
- Triton does not currently emit an inline `fence.sc.cluster` path.

`tensormap.cp_fenceproxy` remains inline because the pinned LLVM revision has no corresponding NVVM operation or LLVM intrinsic. It is a tensor-map copy instruction and requires LLVM support before it can be migrated.

At Triton's pinned LLVM revision, the NVPTX backend maps the new operation to the same `fence.proxy.tensormap::generic.acquire.gpu` PTX instruction.

title: [AMD] Do not insert barriers between mbarrier-synchronized TDM copies
body:
An async copy that carries an mbarrier operand sends an LDS atomic arrive when it completes, so it takes part in mbarrier synchronization exactly like AsyncCopyMbarrierArriveOp, which membarFilter already recognizes. The mbarrier orders those accesses across the whole workgroup, so a ttg.barrier between two such ops synchronizes nothing.

Copies without a barrier operand are deliberately not covered here. Those are ordered by their async wait instead, and an async wait counter is per wave, so it cannot order accesses between waves.

Without this, a TDM collective expressed with mbarrier completion emits more barriers than the async_tdm_wait formulation it replaces, which makes mbarrier unusable as an alternative.

title: [AMD] Make the membar async-load filter direction-aware
body:
The AMD membar filter vetoes the barrier between an async load and a
local_load synced via async_wait regardless of which of the two comes
first.

In the RAW direction (async load, then the synced local_load) the veto
is safe. The load's token proves its copy was waited for, and Membar
already emits a barrier right after that wait, so the copy is visible
to every thread before the read. A barrier in front of the load adds
nothing; any copy still in flight at that point is one the kernel chose
not to wait for, and a barrier cannot complete it either.

In the WAR direction (synced local_load, then an async load refilling
the same buffer) the veto is wrong. The wait covers the read, not what
follows it: other threads may still be reading the buffer when the
refill lands, and only a barrier orders that.

Membar passes the pending (earlier) access as op1 and the current access
as op2, so veto only when the synced local_load is op2. Dropping the
rule altogether would instead put a barrier before every synced
local_load that has an unrelated copy in flight, which multi-stage
pipelines routinely do.

title: Fix FP4 TMA Alignment
body:
## Summary

Use physical storage width for Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) stride alignment. Packed FP4 uses `uint8` storage; using its logical 4-bit width incorrectly rejects a 16-byte row stride. Preserve gathered row indices for activation scales so values and scales use the same source rows.

Without preserving those indices, the H100 pointer-gather path pairs `X[gather[i]]` with `X_scale[i]`, producing numerical mismatches rather than a TMA error (maximum relative error 0.9443 versus 0.02 allowed in one case).

[NVIDIA specifies `globalStrides` in bytes, with 16-byte alignment for ordinary TMA.](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-driver-api/cuda_driver_api/group__CUDA__TENSOR__MEMORY.html)

## Desired features

- Accept packed FP4 tensors whose physical storage strides satisfy ordinary TMA alignment.
- Keep gathered activation values and their block/tensor scales on the same source rows.

## Validation

Tested on NVIDIA GB300 (copy below) and NVIDIA H100 (gathered-scale path) with Triton 3.8.0. The copy below is byte-exact and uses ordinary UINT8 TMA (`fp4_padded=False`). The old alignment expression returned `False`; the patched helper returned `True`. This copy does not validate padded FP4 or matmul.

Run with `triton_kernels` from the checkout:

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl
from triton_kernels.tensor import FP4, is_tma_compliant, make_tma, wrap_torch_tensor


@triton.jit
def copy_packed(src, out):
    tl.store(out + tl.arange(0, 32), src.load([0, 0]).reshape(32))


storage = torch.arange(32, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda").reshape(2, 16)
packed = wrap_torch_tensor(storage, dtype=FP4)
out = torch.empty_like(storage)
kernel = copy_packed[(1,)](make_tma(packed, [2, 32], "dense"), out)

# checks
assert torch.equal(out, storage)
assert "cp.async.bulk.tensor" in kernel.asm["ptx"]
assert is_tma_compliant(packed)  # Fails before this change.
```

## Lines Changed

| Type | Added | Removed | Net |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Tests | 0 | 0 | 0 |

body:
Canonicalize FP32 `arith.divf(a, b)` with constant denominator magnitudes in `[2^-126, 2^126]` to `a * tt.approx_divf(1.0, b)` on NVIDIA. The randomized regression compares raw result bits against `div.full.f32` with the same constant denominator. This checks preservation of the original constant-division behavior; PTXAS can use different reciprocal approximations when the denominator is a runtime value.

title: fix: add missing negation in WSDataPartition thenYieldArg check
body:
## Summary

Fixes #9559

The `thenYieldArg` branch in `getBackwardSliceToPartition` (line 324) was missing the `!` negation operator, causing inverted error handling compared to all other call sites.

## Bug

```cpp
// BEFORE (line 324) — returns false on SUCCESS (wrong)
if (getBackwardSliceToPartition(thenYieldArg, partitionScheme, currentDim))

    return false;
```

All other call sites in the same function use `if (!getBackwardSliceToPartition(...)) return false;` to propagate failure. This was the only one without the negation, as confirmed by @htyu in the issue thread.

Single-character fix — add `!` to match the consistent pattern across the file.

title: Support Python 3.15 and build 3.15t wheels
body:
Adds Python 3.15 support so downstream projects that follow CPython releases (PyTorch is already building 3.15 / 3.15t wheels) are not blocked on Triton.

Two changes, for two different reasons.

## 1. `setup.py`: allow 3.15 to install

```diff
 MIN_PYTHON = (3, 10)
-MAX_PYTHON = (3, 14)
+MAX_PYTHON = (3, 15)
```

This is the actual blocker for 3.15-with-GIL. The existing `cp312-abi3` wheel already runs on 3.15 — `TRITON_STABLE_ABI` sets `Py_LIMITED_API=0x030C0000` and tags the wheel `cp312-abi3`, which is forward compatible — but `python_requires` was `>=3.10,<3.15`, so pip refuses to install it on 3.15. Bumping `MAX_PYTHON` makes it `>=3.10,<3.16` and adds the 3.15 classifier.

**No new non-free-threaded wheel is needed**, and none is added here: the abi3 wheel covers 3.12 through 3.15.

## 2. `wheels.yml`: build a free-threaded 3.15t wheel

Free-threaded builds do not support the limited API, so the cp312 abi3 wheel cannot cover `3.15t` — it needs a version-specific wheel, like the existing cp310/cp311 pass:

```yaml
export CIBW_ENABLE="cpython-prerelease"
export CIBW_BUILD="cp315t-manylinux_${{ matrix.config.arch }}"
export CIBW_ENVIRONMENT="MAX_JOBS=4 TRITON_EXT_ENABLED=ON TRITON_BUILD_WITH_CLANG_LLD=1"
python3 -m cibuildwheel . --output-dir wheelhouse
```

Note `TRITON_STABLE_ABI` is deliberately **not** set for this pass.

### Why `cpython-prerelease`

`manylinux_2_28` currently ships **3.15.0rc1** (`build_cpython315` / `build_cpython315_nogil` stages in pypa/manylinux's Dockerfile), and cibuildwheel gates prerelease CPython behind `CIBW_ENABLE=cpython-prerelease`. The flag can be dropped once the image carries 3.15.0 final. cibuildwheel already knows the identifiers:

```
{ identifier = "cp315t-manylinux_x86_64",  version = "3.15", path_str = "/opt/python/cp315-cp315t" }
{ identifier = "cp315t-manylinux_aarch64", version = "3.15", path_str = "/opt/python/cp315-cp315t" }
```

cibuildwheel's docs caution against publishing prerelease-built wheels to **PyPI**; this workflow publishes to the Triton-Nightly Azure feed, which is the intended consumer for pre-GA testing.

## Scope / follow-ups

- Only `3.15t` is added. `3.13t` and `3.14t` are also uncovered by the abi3 wheel today; adding them is the same one-block change if wanted, but I kept this PR to 3.15.
- The workflow only runs on `schedule`, `workflow_dispatch`, and PRs touching `wheels.yml` — so this PR exercises the new build path in CI.

`getBackwardSliceToPartition` returns `true` when a value can be sliced and `false` when partitioning should fail. The `scf.if` result path handled the else yield with `if (!getBackwardSliceToPartition(...)) return false;`, but the then yield used the opposite polarity. This matters when a warp-specialized value flows through an `scf.if` before reaching a partitioned consumer such as `ttng.warp_group_dot`: the then and else yield operands both have to be followed backward before the result can be sliced.

## What changed

- Make the then-yield recursive check use the same success polarity as the else-yield path.
- Add a `ws_data_partition.mlir` regression where a `ttg.local_alloc` result is yielded through both arms of an `scf.if` and then consumed by `ttng.warp_group_dot`.

There was an earlier closed PR for the one-line code change (#9794). This version adds a focused lit regression and avoids carrying unrelated metadata.

# [mxfp4] ttg::Fp4ToFpOp add support for FP4 upcast to FP32

 ## Motivation

On AMD CDNA3 architecture, upcasting FP4 to BF16 requires first upcasting to FP32 then truncating to BF16. In W4A16(a operand dtype is BF16) kernel calculation:

1. Scale (FP8) needs to be upcast to BF16 to multiply with BF16 weight (from `gl.fp4_to_fp`) for dequantization
2. CDNA3 does not support BF16 multiplication, so BF16 weight has to be upcast back to FP32 for computation
3. The repeated FP32 <-> BF16 conversions cause significant performance overhead

## Change

Add FP4 -> FP32 upcast support to ttg::Fp4ToFpOp, eliminating redundant type conversions and improving kernel performance on AMD CDNA3.

title: Support computation pipelining after SWP refactoring
body:
With the recent SWP refactoring, it is much easier to support arbitrary stage assignments where computations can be separated into different stages. Computation pipelining is basically splitting computations to different stages. Take flash attention as an example:
Currently the two loads are in stage 0 (S0), all other ops are in the last stage (stage 2). The loop body will look like
MMA0(i)
Softmax(i)
MUL(i)
MMA1(i)
LoadV(i+2)
LoadK(i+2)

This patch defines two different pipeline schedule for attention-like kernels:
1> putting first dot in S2, other computations in S3, loadK in stage 0, loadV in stage 1
MMA0(i+1)    
Softmax(i)
MUL(i)
MMA1(i)
loadK(i+3) 
loadV(i+2)
2> putting second dot in S3, other computations in S2, loadK in stage 0, loadV in stage 1
MMA0(i+1)      
MMA1(i)       
Softmax(i+1)   
MUL(i+1)           
loadK(i+3)       
loadV(i+2)

title: Implementation of Computation Pipelining
body:
Summary:
The idea of computation pipelining comes from FA3 paper. The goal is to divide computation ops into stages and to overlap ops that use cuda core with ops that use tensor core.

Use flash attention with num_stages=3 as an example, currently the two loads are in stage 0 (S0), all other ops are in the last stage (stage 2). The loop body will look like
S2(i)      S2(i+1) S2(i+2)
S0(i+2) S0(i+3) S0(i+4)
With computation pipelining enabled, we can put the load for the first dot in S0, the load for the second dot in S1, the first dot in S2, and the rest in S3. The loop body will look like
S2(i+1) S2(i+2) S2(i+3)
S3(i)     S3(i+1) S3(i+2)
S0(i+3) S0(i+4) S0(i+5)
S1(i+2) S1(i+3) S1(i+4)

Note that the distance between the load and the corresponding usage stays the same (i.e 2 stages from the load of k in S0(i+3) to the use in S2(i+3), 2 stages from the load of v in S1(i+2) to the use in S3(i+2)), number of buffers stays at 3. The live range for output of S2 is increased to span the loop (i.e from S2(i+1) to S3(i+1)).

Details:
SWP_FIRST_DOT: move first dot in numStages - 2 instead of numStages - 1
--> for this to work, we need to support predicate on barrier_wait or use PEEL_EPILOGUE
LOAD_DIFFERENT_STAGE: put two loads in two different stages
FIRST_USE_OF_LOAD: only consider the first use of each load, for example load of k is used by the first dot and indirectly used by the 2nd dot, but we should only consider the use by the first dot to calculate the use distance.

For both createAsyncCopy and createTMAAsyncCopy, update TMAUserToWait so there will be an extra dependency from the view of the load to the barrier_wait op:
TMAUserToWait[viewLoad] = waitOp; // viewLoad will depend on barrierWait
In scheduleDependencies, waitOp will be added to the same stage/cluster as viewLoad.

LOAD_DIFFERENT_STAGE=1 FIRST_LOAD_OF_USE=1 SWP_FIRST_DOT=1 together with a TMA variant of FA (https://github.com/pytorch/benchmark/pull/2379) seems to improve performance for headDim 128 and 256.

This implementation is kind of specific to flash attention, and needs rework. We can make it more general by adding a dependency analyzer that analyzes dependency and resource usages of ttgir ops, decides how to break ops into stages, and feeds the decisions to SWP. Another less general option is to only support num_computation_stage being 2 (i.e separate computation ops into two stages). In this restricted form, lifting the first dot into its own stage seems reasonable.

Open to discussions and reworks.

title: [NVIDIA] Lower warp-specialization barriers with NVVM
body:
## Summary

Use the NVVM dialect for the remaining NVIDIA non-mbarrier barrier path instead of manually constructing an LLVM intrinsic call.

Warp-specialization switch loops currently emit `llvm.nvvm.barrier.cta.sync.all` by name. Emitting `nvvm.barrier` keeps the target operation represented in MLIR, uses the dialect verifier, and delegates LLVM intrinsic selection to NVVM translation.

CTA barriers, warp barriers, and cluster arrive/wait barriers elsewhere already use NVVM dialect operations. This change makes the warp-specialization all-participant named barriers consistent with them.

At Triton's pinned LLVM revision, `nvvm.barrier` translates to the same `llvm.nvvm.barrier.cta.sync.all` intrinsic and NVPTX backend instruction, so the emitted `bar.sync` semantics are unchanged.

title: [AMD][Draft] Implement implicit layout conversion for DotOp to enable direct GMEM to reg loads
body:
### Related RFC
[RFC][AMD] Optimizations for Paged Attention: Proposal with Multiple Features(https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/issues/8281)

### [Feature 2] Implicit Layout Conversion
**Problem**  
We found that partitioning the `seq_len` dimension of matrix K and the `head_dim` dimension of matrix V across different wavefronts yields significant benefits (because loading matrices K and V does not require shared memory).  
However, the AMD backend pass of the Triton compiler **does not support directly loading data from global memory into registers and completing a `DotOp` with `DotOperandEncodingAttr`.** Instead, it requires an intermediate transfer through shared memory using `ConvertLayoutOp`.  
The goal of implicit layout conversion is to **directly load data in a layout that matches matrix multiplication requirements,** eliminating unnecessary conversions.  

**Core Process**  
1. Traverse operations until a `DotOp` is matched.  
2. For both operands of the `DotOp`, trace backward until a `LoadOp` is matched, and determine whether implicit layout conversion is feasible based on the types of operations along the path (essentially, implicit conversion cannot be applied if data copying occurs).  
   - For `ConvertLayoutOp` and `LocalLoadOp`-like operations, check whether data copying occurs. If so, implicit conversion is not allowed.  
   - For other operations, currently only `TransOp`, `ReshapeOp`, `LoadOp`, and `ElementwiseOp` are supported.  
3. Extract the innermost vectorization size (`vecSize`) from the `LayoutAttr` of the matched `LoadOp`, and update the `kWidth` in the `LayoutAttr` of the `DotOp` operands.  
   - Certain constraints must be applied to the value of `vecSize`.  
4. Back-propagate the updated `LayoutAttr` from the `DotOp` operands to all operations along the path to the `LoadOp`.  
5. Forward-propagate the updated `LayoutAttr` to all subsequent operations.  
   - If `ConvertLayoutOp` exists, remove it (Step 4 ensures that all operations along the path have consistent layouts).  
   - Insert `ConvertLayoutOp` before and after each operation to ensure legality; these will be removed later by `RemoveLayoutConversions`.

## Summary

Add documentation for `rhs_k_pack` parameter in `dot_scaled` to clarify the FP4 constraint on sm120 architecture.

## Details

As reported in #9678 and confirmed by @masahi, FP4 formats (e2m1, used by MXFP4/NVFP4) require `rhs_k_pack=True` (the default) on sm120 (Blackwell desktop GPUs like GB202/GB203). Using `rhs_k_pack=False` with FP4 inputs on sm120 causes a compilation assertion failure in `MMAv2.cpp`:

This information was not documented, leading to confusing compilation errors for users on sm120 hardware.

Closes #9678

title: [Backend] Recognise reversed mul operands in CombineBroadcastMulReducePattern
body:
CombineBroadcastMulReducePattern folds a broadcast-mul-reduce form into `tt.dot`. After #10545 generalized this combine, the pattern no longer requires explicit `tt.expand_dims` ops: it identifies dot-like operands from broadcasted shapes such as `(M, K, 1) -> (M, K, N)` and `(1, K, N) -> (M, K, N)`.

Since `arith.mulf` is commutative, the two broadcast operands may appear in either order. However, the matcher still assumed that mul operand 0 was the axis-2 broadcast and mul operand 1 was the axis-0 broadcast.

For example, this order is matched:

```mlir
%lhs_b = tt.broadcast %lhs : tensor<32x16x1xf32> -> tensor<32x16x32xf32>
%rhs_b = tt.broadcast %rhs : tensor<1x16x32xf32> -> tensor<32x16x32xf32>
%mul = arith.mulf %lhs_b, %rhs_b : tensor<32x16x32xf32>
%out = "tt.reduce"(%mul) <{axis = 1 : i32}> ...
```

But the equivalent reversed order is missed:

```mlir
%mul = arith.mulf %rhs_b, %lhs_b : tensor<32x16x32xf32>
```

This patch identifies the dot operands from the broadcast axes instead of from the `arith.mulf` operand order. The axis-2 source is still used as the `tt.dot` lhs and the axis-0 source as rhs, so both multiplication orders produce the same `tt.dot`.

This is similar to #10734 in that it removes an unnecessary ordering assumption when matching operands of a commutative operation.

Added 1 lit test in `test/Triton/combine.mlir`, covering the swapped `arith.mulf` operand order in the generalized broadcast-reduce dot combine pattern.

title: [Testing] do_bench: add fixed iteration count option for distributed workloads
body:
Fixes #9683

## Problem

`do_bench` computes `n_warmup` and `n_repeat` by dividing a target duration (e.g. warmup=25ms) by a per-rank timing estimate. In distributed workloads that use collectives such as `all_reduce` or `all_gather`, this produces different iteration counts across ranks due to small timing differences. The rank with more iterations calls the collective one extra time with no matching call on the other side, causing a hang or crash.

## Solution

Add optional `n_warmup` and `n_repeat` parameters so callers can pin the iteration counts directly. When both are provided, the estimation phase is skipped entirely, guaranteeing that every rank executes `fn` the same number of times.

The new parameters default to `None`, preserving the existing time-based behavior for all current callers.

## Example Usage
```python
triton.testing.do_bench(fn, n_warmup=10, n_repeat=50)
```
